paragraphs: §1 — Q narrows the refutation to Daniel; the contradictory-pair argument

He [Daniel al-Qūmisī] is exceedingly prolix on this [theme] in more than one place in his books; and we have already shown, in the seventh bab of the Maqala that precedes this one, the establishing of the authority of reason (ḥujjat al-ʿaql) and the invalidation of the statement of whoever rejected it — by that which is binding upon Daniel and upon others. Save that here we refute him in particular, and so we say: it is not admissible that two mutually-contrary things (shayʾāni mutaḍāddāni) be both alike blameworthy; rather, everything that is blameworthy, its contrary — which is its opposite — must necessarily be praiseworthy. And this is the contrary of what he alleges and openly declares, namely the obligatoriness of investigation, inquiry (al-baḥth wa-l-naẓar), and the employment of analogical reasoning (al-qiyās), which is the gateway of the intelligible (bāb al-maʿqūl).

: The bab is a targeted, ad hominem sequel to Maqala II's general defense of reason (Q's explicit back-reference, "the seventh bab of the Maqala before this one," = M2 B7, ithbāt ḥujjat al-ʿaql). The adversary, Daniel al-Qūmisī (late-9th-c. Karaite of Damaghan/Jerusalem, founder of the Karaite "Mourners of Zion" movement), held a scripturalist position hostile to kalām-style rational theology — a stance Q the Bahshamī-rationalist Karaite finds untenable. The opening argument is a neat logical squeeze: if rational inquiry (al-naẓar) is, as Daniel says, blameworthy, then its contrary — ignorance (al-jahl, the majhūl) — must be praiseworthy, which is absurd. The principle that contraries cannot share a single evaluative valence (a thing and its opposite cannot both be blameworthy) is a kalām commonplace, here turned against the anti-rationalist. al-naẓar fī al-maʿqūl and al-qiyās are the anchor terms (glossary §III); Q's gloss "bāb al-maʿqūl" ("the gateway of the intelligible") names rational inquiry as the very instrument Daniel would shut.
§2 — The anthropomorphism dilemma: rejecting reason forces a corporeal God

It also follows upon him that he must allow of the Creator (mighty and exalted be He) that He is a body (jism), and that He is possessed of limbs and instruments (dhā jawāriḥ wa-ālāt) — since Scripture is filled with reports to this effect; and it is only from the standpoint of the intelligible (min jihat al-maʿqūl) that the professors of the divine unity (al-muwaḥḥida) have negated all these descriptions of Him. So if the intelligible is blameworthy, and inquiry into it neither obligatory nor even admissible, and the only thing that is obligatory is the following of Scripture alone, and Scripture speaks with what we have mentioned of the corporealist likening (al-tashbīh) — then it is not admissible for Daniel to allege of the Creator (mighty and majestic) anything other than that. And should he plead the saying of Scripture [Deut 4:15] כִּי לֹא רְאִיתֶם כָּל תְּמוּנָה ("for you saw no form") and the like of it, it is said to him: not everything from which the resemblance of some other thing is negated must therefore be at variance with its likeness in every respect; for it is admissible that His negation of the likening from Himself be [a negation drawn] from [the standpoint of] the bigness of the body, its intensity, its strength, and its beauty — since people often use that [manner of speaking] in their discourse. So you — from where did you say that He does not resemble [a body] in every respect, when you do not affirm the intelligible nor hold by it?

: The decisive tu quoque. Q impales Daniel on the consequence of his own scripturalism: Scripture is replete with anthropomorphic language (God's "limbs and instruments," sitting, walking, etc.); the only ground on which the muwaḥḥida (the strict monotheists — Karaite and Muʿtazilī) strip these of literal force is al-maʿqūl (reason). Banish reason and follow the bare letter, and you are committed to a corporeal God (tashbīh) — exactly the heresy Daniel would reject. When Daniel pleads the anti-anthropomorphic Deut 4:15 ("you saw no form"), Q turns it back: a negation of likeness need not be a negation in every respect (it could merely deny that God shares a body's magnitude, intensity, strength, beauty); so Daniel cannot derive a categorical, in-every-respect transcendence from the verse without invoking the very rational principle he disowns. al-tashbīh (anthropomorphism) is the same target Q treated in Maqala II (cf. Bab 6 §2's back-reference to it).
§3 — The few anti-likeness verses vs. the many anthropomorphic ones; the "eye" and "ear" challenge

And further: what is in Scripture by way of the negation of likening is [only] two places, or three; whereas what is in it by way of necessitating that the Creator be seen, and that He is possessed of instruments and limbs, and that He sits, and is turned back, and goes, and comes, and stands, and other than that of this kind — is so much as not to be numbered. So you — why have you set the two or three places upon the literal sense of the saying (ẓāhir al-qawl), and interpreted the greater number away from the literal sense (ghayr al-ẓāhir)? And it is said to him: are you able to point out, in the whole of Scripture, an "eye" conjoined with which is the predicate that it is not a limb, or an "ear" conjoined with which is [a] hearing [that is] not [by] a limb? For you will not find that. And since that is so, it is said to him: then why have you alleged that the saying of the Prophet [Ps 94:9] הֲנֹטַע אֹזֶן הֲלֹא יִשְׁמָע אִם יֹצֵר עַיִן הֲלֹא יַבִּיט ("He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? He who formed the eye, shall He not see?") — that by this he does not intend an ear and an eye that are limbs — and you have interpreted upon it (taʾawwalta ʿalayhi) the contrary of what the language [actually] admits? And the like of that is binding upon him in respect of what Scripture has spoken that suggests multiplicity / bigness (al-kathra / al-kibar) and other than it, of what does not befit the [true] religion — of that whose corruption is known only from the standpoint of the intelligible.

: A quantitative-then-qualitative thrust. (1) Quantitative: the anti-anthropomorphic verses are a mere handful ("two or three"), the anthropomorphic ones beyond count — so Daniel, who does read the few non-literally while taking the many literally, is already practising the figurative interpretation (taʾwīl) he condemns, and on the inferior textual evidence at that. (2) Qualitative: Q challenges Daniel to find a single verse where Scripture itself glosses "eye" or "ear" as non-corporeal — there is none; the non-corporeal reading of, e.g., Ps 94:9 ("He who planted the ear … formed the eye") comes only from reason, not from the text. So Daniel's own anti-anthropomorphism silently depends on al-maʿqūl. The bracketed `al-kathra / al-kibar` reflects the source's own variant (the OCR marks a slash, "multiplicity / bigness," at this point — see Translator's notes). The phrase taʾawwalta ʿalayhi khilāfa mā taḥtamiluhu al-lugha ("you interpreted upon it contrary to what the language admits") is Q's standing formula for an interpretation that violates the ẓāhir — the same taʾwīl-must-agree-with-the-ẓāhir hermeneutic Q deploys against the Christians in Bab 6 §1, here turned against a fellow Karaite.
§4 — The trustworthiness of prophecy and of true vs. false report cannot stand without reason

Then he is asked about what the Christians (al-naṣārā) hold of the hypostases (al-aqānīm), and about what they adduce as proof from Scripture for it; and likewise he is asked about the prophets — from where their authority (ḥujja) is established, and by what means a distinction is drawn between מֹשֶׁה and between so-and-so (fulān), and from where the prophethood of the one of them is established and the prophethood of the other invalidated — given that we have witnessed neither one of them. And if he pleads the [transmitted] report (al-khabar), he is countered with the report of the other; then it is said to him: and is a differentiation admissible between the sound report and the false report (al-khabar al-ṣaḥīḥ wa-l-khabar al-bāṭil) save by the intelligible (al-maʿqūl)? And that which is against him in this is so much as not to be numbered.

: The closing reductio extends the same logic to two further domains, both fatal for a thoroughgoing anti-rationalism. (a) Anti-Christian polemic: how can Daniel refute the Christians' scriptural prooftexts for the aqānīm (hypostases) — the very task of Babs 5–6 — without rational argument? (b) Prophetology: how distinguish a true prophet (מֹשֶׁה, Moses) from a pretender ("so-and-so," fulān) when neither was witnessed by us? Appeal to al-khabar (transmitted report) is no escape, since the false claimant has his report too; only al-maʿqūl can adjudicate the sound report (al-khabar al-ṣaḥīḥ) from the false one (al-bāṭil). This anticipates the prophetology of M3 B15–16 (glossary §VII, nubuwwa / muʿjiza). The bab closes on the formulaic "so much as not to be numbered" (kathīr lā yuḥṣā), Q's tag for an objection he regards as overwhelming.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is explicit: ʿalā Dāniyāl al-Qūmisī fī inkārihi li-l-naẓar fī al-maʿqūl — "against Daniel al-Qūmisī, concerning his rejection of inquiry into the intelligible." This is the second of a small run of babs Q directs by name at Daniel al-Qūmisī (Bab 22 then takes up Daniel's denial of angels), marking the structural pivot from the anti-Christian polemic of Babs 1–18 (and the resurrection/eschatology block) to intra-Karaite controversy with the scripturalist wing of Q's own movement. Daniel al-Qūmisī (fl. c. 880, Damaghan → Jerusalem) was a founding figure of the Jerusalem Karaite "Mourners of Zion" and an opponent of speculative theology; Q, who builds his entire system on Bahshamī kalām, finds Daniel's anti-rationalism self-undermining.

- The single argumentative engine. The whole bab runs on one move, applied four times: Daniel's own commitments secretly require the reason he rejects. (§1) If reason is blameworthy, ignorance is praiseworthy — absurd. (§2) Reject reason and the literal text gives you a corporeal God. (§3) Daniel already reads the few anti-anthropomorphic verses non-literally — that is the taʾwīl/reason he condemns; and no verse glosses "eye/ear" as non-corporeal without reason supplying it. (§4) Neither anti-Christian refutation nor the authentication of prophecy (true vs. false khabar) is possible without reason. Each is a clean ad hominem (in the technical, non-pejorative sense): Q does not re-prove the authority of reason here — he did that in M2 B7, to which §1 refers — but shows that Daniel cannot consistently deny it.

- Reason and the ẓāhir. Note the deftness of §3: Q does not oppose reason to the plain sense (ẓāhir) but shows that Daniel's selective literalism (literal for the many anthropomorphic verses, figurative for the few transcendence verses) is itself a rational triage — so Daniel is a closet rationalist. This is the same taʾwīl-must-track-the-ẓāhir-as-disciplined-by-reason hermeneutic Q wields against Christian typology in Bab 6 §1, here turned inward against a co-religionist. The verb taʾawwala ʿalā ("to interpret [a sense] onto" a text) carries Q's disapproval: an interpretation imposed against what "the language admits" (mā taḥtamiluhu al-lugha).

- The Ps 94:9 prooftext. Q's instance — "He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? He who formed the eye, shall He not see?" (Ps 94:9) — is well chosen: it is precisely a verse where Scripture predicates ear and eye of God, and which Daniel must (and does) read non-corporeally; Q's point is that nothing in the verse licenses the non-corporeal reading — only al-maʿqūl does. The OCR-recovered Hebrew here (see below) is הֲנֹטַע אֹזֶן הֲלֹא יִשְׁמָע אִם יֹצֵר עַיִן הֲלֹא יַבִּיט.

- OCR note (the diff-report). The multimodal re-OCR corrected one substantive Hebrew run that Kraken had garbled: at §2 the citation כִּי לֹא רְאִיתֶם כָּל תְּמוּנָה [Deut 4:15] (Kraken read a meaningless `ישעי טג`). The merged text used here is the multimodal reading and is sound. Three further Kraken "Hebrew" runs flagged in the diff-report (`יח`, `ואל מי תדמיון אל`, `יימו`) were spurious in Kraken and absent in the multimodal pass; they are not part of the Arabic text and have been excluded — note, however, that `ואל מי תדמיון אל` is Isa 40:25 ("to whom then will you liken Me?"), an anti-likeness verse thematically apt to this bab, so it is possible Q cited it in §3 (the "two or three places" of anti-likeness verses) and the multimodal pass dropped it; flagged as a possible lacuna for the edition. The one place where the source itself is uncertain is §3's `الكثرة / الكبر` ("multiplicity / bigness"), where the merged text carries a slash marking two readings; rendered with both, since either fits ("Scripture's language that suggests plurality or magnitude in God").

For Qūmisī's own works, see Jacob Mann's editions of the Pitron Shenem ʿAsar fragments. - For Q's general defense of rational inquiry (the §1 back-reference): Maqala II, Bab 7 (ithbāt ḥujjat al-ʿaql) of the Anwār — the systematic proof to which this bab is the ad hominem sequel; cf. Maqala I, Bab 1 (the obligatoriness of al-naẓar). See `anchor_grid_M3` ad loc. - For the Bahshamī Muʿtazilī apparatus behind al-naẓar / al-qiyās / ḥujjat al-ʿaql: ʿAbd al-Jabbār, Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa (the obligatoriness of al-naẓar as first duty) and al-Mughnī vol. 12 (al-Naẓar wa-l-Maʿārif); glossary §III anchor terms (al-ʿaql, al-naẓar, al-burhān, al-qiyās). - For the anti-anthropomorphism (tashbīh) argument Q presupposes (§2): Q's own Anwār Maqala II treatment of al-tashbīh (the back-reference shared with Bab 6 §2); for the broader Karaite–Muʿtazilī rejection of divine corporeality, Georges Vajda and Ben-Shammai on Qirqisānī's theology, and ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. 5 (al-Firaq).
